dataset_name: PotWise Plant Problem Helper — Research Draft
status: initial research draft — review before production use
intended_use: Rule-based, cautious screening and follow-up questions for 15 supported plants; not a validated diagnostic system.
design_principle: Plant-specific symptom evidence + user observations + actual conditions + season/weather context. Do not use season as a proxy for pot moisture.
global_diagnostic_policy: This database is a screening aid, not a definitive plant disease diagnosis.
Never map a single symptom to a single cause without considering alternate explanations.
For every watering recommendation, check moisture in the root zone, drainage and actual rain exposure before suggesting water.
Use season and weather as context only; never infer that rain reached a pot or that a plant needs more/less water from month alone.

Prefer low-risk cultural steps: observe, inspect, isolate suspected pests, improve confirmed drainage/airflow issues, and remove clearly dead material. Avoid pesticide specifics unless pest identity, local registration, crop context and product-label directions are verified.
When symptoms are severe, rapidly spreading, or diagnosis remains uncertain, recommend a local horticulture extension service, nursery specialist, or plant clinic.
Distinguish plant-specific evidence from general indoor-plant pest or light guidance in UI wording.
Do not claim that a listed symptom proves a named disease; use language like “possible cause” and explain which clues support it.

seasonal_context_rules.label: Hot, dry spell / heatwave
check_first: Check root-zone moisture rather than surface appearance alone.
Ask whether the plant receives direct sun, hot wind, or heat reflecting off a wall.
Check for scorch and wilting, but do not assume water is always the cause.
seasonal_context_rules.interpretation: High heat and stronger light can increase water use for some plants and increase scorch risk; response varies by species, pot, substrate, and exposure.
must_not_assume: Do not automatically increase watering solely because it is summer.
Do not move a shade-adapted plant suddenly into intense direct sun.

seasonal_context_rules.label: Rainy spell / prolonged wet weather
check_first: Ask whether rain actually reaches this pot; a covered balcony or indoor plant may receive none.
Check moisture below the surface and whether drainage holes are clear.
Check if the saucer/cachepot holds water and whether foliage stays wet for long periods.
seasonal_context_rules.interpretation: Rain exposure and slow drying can make excess moisture more plausible, but a rainy forecast does not prove that a particular pot is wet.
must_not_assume: Do not assume every pot received rain during monsoon or a rainy season.
Do not water or withhold water based only on a seasonal label; inspect the mix.

seasonal_context_rules.label: Cooler period / reduced light
check_first: Check whether growth has slowed and how long the mix now takes to dry.
Review available daylight and any new cold drafts.
Compare current conditions with the plant-specific needs.
seasonal_context_rules.interpretation: Lower light often slows growth and water use, so soil may dry more slowly. Seasonal rules should influence questions, not impose a fixed watering schedule.
must_not_assume: Do not use a universal winter watering frequency for all species and climates.
Do not treat slow growth alone as disease.

seasonal_context_rules.label: Recent move / abrupt light or temperature change
check_first: Ask about relocation, repotting, open windows, heating/cooling airflow, and sudden sun exposure.
Look for scorch, bud drop, or symptoms concentrated on exposed tissue.
seasonal_context_rules.interpretation: A recent environmental change can explain some leaf/bud drop or scorch; change only one care factor at a time and observe new growth.
must_not_assume: Do not immediately add fertilizer or pesticide without supporting clues.

seasonal_context_rules.label: Warm and humid, but little/no actual rain
check_first: Do not infer root wetness from humidity alone.
Check actual soil moisture, airflow, pest signs and whether foliage stays wet.
seasonal_context_rules.interpretation: Humidity and rain exposure are distinct variables. High humidity may affect drying and disease risk for some plants, but pot moisture must be observed directly.
must_not_assume: Do not equate high humidity with a watered root zone.
Do not mark a rain-exposed plant unless the user confirms exposure.

problems.display_title: Soft, yellowing or water-soaked leaves

possible_causes.cause: Excess moisture or poor drainage; root damage is possible
supporting_clues: Potting mix remains wet for an unusually long time
Leaf base or roots are soft/brown rather than firm
Pot lacks drainage holes or excess water collects in a cachepot

possible_causes.cause: Leaf spot or another disease
supporting_clues: Distinct lesions persist or spread despite correcting watering
Spots are black or otherwise patterned rather than uniform yellowing

follow_up_questions: How long has the soil stayed wet?
Are the leaves firm, or soft/mushy?
Does the pot drain freely?
Are spots spreading to new leaves?
safe_next_steps: Check moisture below the surface before watering again.
Confirm the pot has working drainage and empty collected runoff.
If inspecting roots, look for soft, dark, decayed roots; seek local horticulture advice if lesions keep spreading.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not recommend extra water based on drooping alone.
Do not label a leaf spot as a confirmed fungal disease from an image alone.
problems.evidence_notes: Both moisture stress and leaf disease/pests can produce spots; symptom alone is insufficient.

problems.display_title: Spots plus visible insects or cottony material

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs or aphids; scale, mites or leaf-spot diseases are also possible
supporting_clues: White cottony clusters on leaf bases or undersides
Visible insects or persistent lesions

follow_up_questions: Can you see insects or cottony material at the leaf base or underside?
Are lesions spreading, or are they stable?
safe_next_steps: Isolate the plant from nearby plants while checking it.
Inspect leaf bases and undersides; remove only badly affected tissue with clean tools when needed.
Use a plant-specific, locally approved control only after the pest is identified.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not apply a pesticide mixture or household chemical without correct identification and label directions.

problems.display_title: Yellowing leaves or leaf drop

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering/root stress
supporting_clues: Mix remains damp or saturated
Drainage is poor
Roots are brown, soft or sparse if inspected

possible_causes.cause: Low light or normal ageing of older leaves
supporting_clues: Only the oldest leaves yellow gradually
Plant receives very little usable light
No pests are visible and remaining growth looks healthy

follow_up_questions: Are the yellow leaves mostly older leaves near the base or new leaves?
Does the mix feel wet, slightly moist, or dry below the surface?
How much natural or grow light reaches the plant?
safe_next_steps: Check moisture before watering; pothos should not stay constantly damp.
Empty runoff from a saucer or decorative outer pot.
If yellowing continues, inspect the undersides and review light level.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not treat every older yellow leaf as a disease.
Do not water by a fixed calendar if the mix is still damp.
problems.evidence_notes: The sources explicitly note several possible causes and normal ageing of older leaves.

problems.display_title: Brown tips, margins or leaf spots

possible_causes.cause: Inconsistent watering or excess fertilizer/salt buildup
supporting_clues: Tips or edges brown; watering alternates between very dry and wet
Recent or frequent fertilizer use

possible_causes.cause: Pest or disease damage
supporting_clues: Spots spread to new leaves
Pests or feeding marks appear underneath leaves

follow_up_questions: Has the plant recently been fertilized or sprayed?
Do spots appear on new leaves?
Can you see pests underneath leaves?
safe_next_steps: Check the recent watering and fertilizer history.
Inspect leaf undersides; remove severely spotted leaves only if needed.
Avoid routine leaf misting; improve general care and monitor whether new damage appears.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume all brown spots are pests or infection.
Do not suggest an unverified home spray.

problems.display_title: Sparse, stretched or leggy vines

possible_causes.cause: Insufficient usable light
supporting_clues: Vines stretch toward a light source
Growth becomes sparse or weak
Plant has only dim room light

follow_up_questions: Does the plant lean toward a window or lamp?
Has its light exposure changed with the season?
safe_next_steps: Move it gradually to brighter appropriate indirect light or add suitable grow lighting.
Rotate periodically for more even exposure.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not move it suddenly into harsh direct sun; acclimate gradually.

problems.display_title: White powdery coating on leaves or shoots

possible_causes.cause: Possible powdery mildew
supporting_clues: Powder-like white growth on leaf surfaces or young shoots
New leaves appear distorted

follow_up_questions: Does the white material look powdery and recur after gentle wiping?
Are young leaves or shoots distorted?
Is the plant crowded with poor airflow?
safe_next_steps: Remove heavily affected fallen or detached material.
Improve spacing and airflow and avoid keeping the foliage persistently wet.
Seek local plant-diagnostic advice if it spreads or affects many plants.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not claim confirmed mildew from a photo alone.
Do not recommend chemical treatment rates copied from field-crop guidance for a potted household plant.
problems.evidence_notes: TNAU lists powdery mildew; the safe steps are conservative cultural measures, not chemical prescriptions.

problems.display_title: Rolled leaves or chewed young growth

possible_causes.cause: Leaf-roller or other leaf-feeding insect activity
supporting_clues: Leaves are folded/rolled together
Chewing marks or larvae are visible inside rolled leaves

follow_up_questions: Are leaves rolled around a visible insect or silk?
Can you see larvae, frass, or fresh chewing?
safe_next_steps: Inspect rolled leaves and leaf undersides.
On a small potted plant, remove clearly infested leaves or visible pests by hand and monitor new growth.
Confirm the pest before choosing any treatment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not spray broad-spectrum pesticide without identifying the pest.
problems.evidence_notes: TNAU identifies leaf rollers as a minor Tulsi pest; hand-removal is a conservative screening action.

problems.display_title: Wilting or decline while soil stays wet

possible_causes.cause: Excess water, drainage problems or root/seedling disease
supporting_clues: Soil remains saturated
Plant wilts despite wet soil
Stem base or roots look dark/soft

possible_causes.cause: Underwatering or heat stress
supporting_clues: Root zone is dry and pot is light
Symptoms follow a hot, dry spell

follow_up_questions: Is the soil wet or dry several centimetres down?
Does water drain from the pot?
Was there recent rain or a heat spell?
safe_next_steps: Check root-zone moisture and drainage before adding water.
Keep the plant out of standing water; remove a badly collapsed seedling and inspect nearby plants.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume wilt always means thirst.
Do not treat root rot or seedling blight as confirmed without stronger evidence.

problems.display_title: Yellow, soft or collapsing leaves near the base

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering or root/rhizome rot
supporting_clues: Mix remains wet between waterings
Leaf bases become soft or mushy
Pot drainage is poor

possible_causes.cause: Natural ageing of an isolated older leaf
supporting_clues: One older leaf changes slowly while other leaves remain firm

follow_up_questions: Is the affected leaf one of the oldest, or are several leaves affected?
Is the potting mix completely dry, moist, or wet?
Are leaf bases firm?
safe_next_steps: Check the mix and drainage before watering.
Allow the mix to dry appropriately for this drought-tolerant plant.
If the base is soft or decline is spreading, inspect roots/rhizomes and seek help if needed.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not water on a weekly schedule regardless of soil condition.
Do not assume one slowly dying older leaf means whole-plant disease.

problems.display_title: Cottony pests, fine webbing or bleached/scorched patches

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs or spider mites
supporting_clues: Cottony clusters near leaf bases
Fine webbing or tiny moving specks

possible_causes.cause: Light scorch after strong direct sun
supporting_clues: Bleached or dry patches on sun-facing leaves after a sudden light change

follow_up_questions: Can you see cottony material or webbing?
Was the plant moved into stronger sun recently?
safe_next_steps: Inspect leaf bases and undersides; isolate if pests are suspected.
If scorch followed sudden sun exposure, return to suitable bright indirect/partial light and acclimate gradually.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not treat scorch as infectious disease without supporting clues.

problems.display_title: Brown or crispy leaf tips

possible_causes.cause: Water-quality sensitivity (salts/chlorine/fluoride), too little water, or low humidity
supporting_clues: Tip burn repeats on otherwise healthy strap-like leaves
Tap water is used consistently
Plant has dried too far between waterings or air is very dry

follow_up_questions: What water do you use?
Do tips brown across many leaves or only older leaves?
Does the soil dry completely for long periods?
safe_next_steps: Check watering consistency and root-zone moisture.
Where practical, try rainwater or another suitable low-mineral water source if the source water may be contributing.
Trim only dead tips for appearance; existing brown tissue will not turn green again.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume brown tips prove a nutrient deficiency.
Do not over-fertilize to correct tip burn.

problems.display_title: Scorched leaves or decline in soggy soil

possible_causes.cause: Direct-sun scorch
supporting_clues: Bleached/brown patches occur on leaves exposed to strong direct sun

possible_causes.cause: Waterlogging/root rot
supporting_clues: Mix is persistently wet
Plant declines despite wet soil
Roots are soft/dark

follow_up_questions: Is it in strong direct sun?
Does the pot drain freely?
Is the root zone still wet several days after watering?
safe_next_steps: Use medium or indirect light appropriate to the plant.
Correct blocked drainage and let soil moisture guide watering.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not solve sun scorch by fertilizing.
Do not add water to a plant that is already wilted in wet soil.

problems.display_title: Yellowing leaflets or an entire stalk turning yellow

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering/root stress
supporting_clues: Mix stays wet
Several leaflets or stalks yellow together
Base or roots may be soft

possible_causes.cause: Natural ageing of an older leaf
supporting_clues: Only the oldest leaf is gradually yellowing and other growth is healthy

possible_causes.cause: Less commonly, under-watering or nutrient issue
supporting_clues: Mix is very dry for an extended period, or there is a long history without suitable feeding

follow_up_questions: Is the affected stalk one of the oldest?
Has the mix dried fully since its last watering?
Are several stalks affected?
safe_next_steps: Check the mix before watering; ZZ plants store water and tolerate dry periods.
If soil stays wet or the stalk base is soft, check drainage and roots.
Monitor whether new symptoms develop.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not diagnose nutrient deficiency from yellowing alone.
Do not increase watering solely because a leaflet is yellow.
problems.evidence_notes: Yellowing is nonspecific and can also be normal ageing.

problems.display_title: Scale insects or soft/rotting base

possible_causes.cause: Scale insects
supporting_clues: Fixed raised brown bumps attached to leaves/stems

possible_causes.cause: Root/rhizome rot from persistently wet, poorly aerated mix
supporting_clues: Softened base or roots and a long-lasting wet mix

follow_up_questions: Do raised bumps stay attached when gently examined?
Is the base firm or soft?
Is the soil compacted or waterlogged?
safe_next_steps: Isolate if pests are suspected and inspect nearby plants.
Correct chronic waterlogging; seek help if the rhizome/base is rotting.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not scrape aggressively or apply a pesticide before confirming scale.

problems.display_title: Leaves dropping, soft or yellow leaves

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering/root rot
supporting_clues: Mix remains wet
Leaves drop while soil is damp
Roots are soft/dark if inspected

possible_causes.cause: Underwatering or root stress
supporting_clues: Mix is very dry and leaves look wrinkled/shriveled

follow_up_questions: Is the mix wet, dry, or somewhere between?
Are leaves firm, wrinkled, or soft/translucent?
Does the pot have drainage holes?
safe_next_steps: Check moisture and drainage before watering.
Use a well-drained succulent-appropriate mix and allow it to dry between waterings.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not water just because leaves have fallen; both wet and dry root problems are possible.

problems.display_title: Visible sap-feeding pests on stems or leaves

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs, scale, aphids or spider mites
supporting_clues: Cottony wax, attached bumps, tiny insects, or fine webbing on leaf undersides/stems

follow_up_questions: Are there cottony clusters, raised bumps, sticky residue, or webbing?
Are nearby plants affected too?
safe_next_steps: Separate the plant while inspecting.
Check stem joints and leaf undersides; use identification-specific, locally approved control only if pests are confirmed.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not use broad pesticide mixtures without confirming the pest and label suitability.

problems.display_title: Speckled, yellowing fronds or visible pests

possible_causes.cause: Spider mites, whiteflies or scale
supporting_clues: Fine webbing/tiny specks on undersides
Small white insects fly up when foliage is disturbed
Fixed scale-like bumps on stems or leaves

follow_up_questions: Can you see webbing, moving specks, white flying insects or attached bumps?
Are the undersides more affected?
safe_next_steps: Inspect leaf undersides and stems with good light.
Isolate the plant if pests are plausible and monitor nearby plants.
Confirm the pest before selecting treatment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not infer spider mites from yellowing alone.

problems.display_title: Brown tips or frond decline

possible_causes.cause: Environmental stress or unsuitable indoor humidity/light; watering problems also need checking
supporting_clues: Air is very dry or light/temperature changed recently
Soil stays either saturated or dry for a long period
No visible pests but symptoms continue

follow_up_questions: Has the plant been moved or exposed to a draft or heat source?
Is the potting mix wet or dry below the surface?
Is the indoor air unusually dry?
safe_next_steps: Check moisture and drainage, and keep conditions warm and appropriately bright.
Inspect for pests before assuming the environment is the only cause.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assign a single cause to brown tips without checking water, pests and conditions.
problems.evidence_notes: The cited plant profile supports humidity and pest susceptibility; tip-browning cause is a differential screen requiring stronger follow-up evidence.

problems.display_title: Brown leaf tips or margins

possible_causes.cause: Direct sun, underwatering, low humidity or fertilizer-salt buildup
supporting_clues: Plant receives direct sun
Mix dries excessively
Air is dry
Recent or frequent fertilizer use

follow_up_questions: Does it receive direct sunlight?
Is the mix dry or still moist?
Has fertilizer been applied recently?
safe_next_steps: Keep it in suitable shade/indirect light.
Check moisture before watering and allow excess water to drain.
If over-fertilization is plausible, pause feeding and review product directions rather than adding more fertilizer.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not diagnose a specific nutrient deficiency from brown tips alone.

problems.display_title: Drooping or yellowing leaves

possible_causes.cause: Underwatering or water stress
supporting_clues: Mix is dry and the plant has recently wilted

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering/root stress
supporting_clues: Mix remains wet/soggy yet the plant stays wilted

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs
supporting_clues: Cottony white clusters on leaf undersides or stems

follow_up_questions: Is the soil dry, moist, or wet?
Does the plant perk up after watering when the soil is dry?
Can you see cottony insects underneath leaves?
safe_next_steps: Use the soil check to decide whether water is needed.
Ensure excess water drains away.
Inspect under broad leaves for pests.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not water automatically when a plant wilts in already wet soil.

problems.display_title: Dark leaf spots with yellowing and leaf drop

possible_causes.cause: Possible rose black spot
supporting_clues: Black lesions with feathery/irregular margins
Yellow tissue around lesions
Affected leaves drop early

follow_up_questions: Are spots dark and irregular with yellowing around them?
Are lower or older leaves affected first?
Does foliage often stay wet or are plants crowded?
safe_next_steps: Remove fallen/infected leaves and badly affected canes where appropriate.
Improve spacing and airflow; water the soil rather than repeatedly wetting foliage.
If the problem progresses, seek local plant-diagnostic advice.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not identify black spot from any dark spot alone.
Do not use fungicide without label directions and confirming local suitability.
problems.evidence_notes: The symptom pattern closely follows TNAU description; environmental context helps but does not confirm diagnosis.

problems.display_title: White or gray powder on young leaves, shoots or buds

possible_causes.cause: Possible powdery mildew
supporting_clues: Powdery coating on young leaves/shoots/buds
Leaves may distort and flower buds may open poorly
Conditions include mild temperature and humid nights with drier days, per TNAU

follow_up_questions: Does the coating look powdery on leaf surfaces or buds?
Are young leaves distorted?
Is airflow limited or is the plant shaded?
safe_next_steps: Remove heavily affected fallen material.
Improve airflow and light appropriate for the rose; avoid crowding.
Ask a local horticultural expert if spread is rapid.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not diagnose mildew from dust or spray residue alone.

problems.display_title: Distorted young growth or visible pests

possible_causes.cause: Aphids, thrips or mites are plausible; rose pests vary
supporting_clues: Insects clustered on new shoots/buds
Tiny pests with silvery/bronzed feeding marks
Fine webbing with stippling

follow_up_questions: Are insects visible on buds or new shoots?
Is there webbing or silvery damage?
safe_next_steps: Inspect buds, leaf undersides and tender new growth.
Use non-chemical physical removal where practical and seek pest-specific advice if infestation persists.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume every distorted bud is a pest issue.
Do not recommend pesticide until pest identification is more confident.

problems.display_title: Buds or leaves drop after a move or environmental change

possible_causes.cause: Environmental change or stress following relocation
supporting_clues: Plant was recently moved
Light, temperature, watering or wind exposure changed

follow_up_questions: Was the plant moved or repotted recently?
Did light exposure or temperature change?
Are pests or leaf spots also visible?
safe_next_steps: Keep conditions consistent while checking moisture and pest clues.
Avoid repeatedly moving the plant as a first response.
Monitor new growth before making several changes at once.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume every dropped bud indicates a fertilizer deficiency.

problems.display_title: Raised bumps or sticky residues on leaves/stems

possible_causes.cause: Scale insects are a possible cause
supporting_clues: Fixed raised bumps on stems or leaf veins
Honeydew/sticky residue or yellowing around infested areas

follow_up_questions: Are the bumps attached and difficult to dislodge?
Is there sticky residue or black sooty growth?
Are nearby plants affected?
safe_next_steps: Inspect stems and leaf undersides; isolate the plant if scale is suspected.
Confirm the pest and then choose a treatment suitable for hibiscus and the growing environment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not scrape or spray aggressively without confirming the pest.

problems.display_title: Wilting or stem/root decline in wet soil

possible_causes.cause: Water stagnation, root/stem rot or wilt disease is possible
supporting_clues: Soil stays waterlogged
Stem base is soft/dark
Several plants decline under similar wet conditions

possible_causes.cause: Dry soil or heat stress
supporting_clues: Root zone is dry after hot weather
Leaves recover after appropriate watering

follow_up_questions: Is the soil actually wet or dry?
Does the pot/bed drain?
Is the stem base firm or soft?
safe_next_steps: Avoid standing water and correct drainage.
Remove collapsed plant material and inspect neighbouring plants.
If wilt spreads despite correcting moisture, get plant-diagnostic help.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not prescribe more water solely because the plant wilts.
Do not treat a wilt disease as confirmed without evidence.

problems.display_title: Leaf spots, powdery coating or flower blight

possible_causes.cause: Possible leaf spot, powdery mildew or botrytis-type disease
supporting_clues: Distinct expanding spots or powdery growth
Affected leaves/flowers deteriorate over time

follow_up_questions: Are the lesions discrete spots or a powdery film?
Do affected areas spread after wet weather?
Are plants crowded with poor airflow?
safe_next_steps: Remove fallen/dying material and improve airflow.
Water the growing medium rather than frequently wetting foliage.
Seek local diagnosis if the problem spreads quickly.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not call all spots fungal; insects and environmental injury can look similar.

problems.display_title: Distorted young leaves or sticky/curling shoots

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs or thrips are possible
supporting_clues: White cottony insects and honeydew/sooty growth
Distorted tender tissue or papery feeding damage

follow_up_questions: Are white cottony insects visible on young shoots?
Is growth distorted, rolled or papery?
Are there tiny insects inside flowers or buds?
safe_next_steps: Inspect new growth and flower heads.
Remove a small number of visible pests by hand where practical and monitor.
Confirm the pest before using a control product.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not copy field-crop pesticide rates into a household-pot recommendation.

problems.display_title: Chewed or skeletonized leaves

possible_causes.cause: Leaf-feeding insects, including a reported curry-leaf tortoise beetle, may be involved
supporting_clues: Fresh chewing damage
Visible beetles or larvae on affected leaves

follow_up_questions: Can you see beetles or larvae on the damaged leaves?
Is damage fresh and increasing?
Are only some leaves affected or is the whole plant declining?
safe_next_steps: Inspect leaves, including the undersides, and manually remove visible pests on a small plant when practical.
Photograph the insect and damage for identification before selecting a treatment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume all leaf holes are the tortoise beetle; the cited Indian report documents an outbreak, not universal prevalence.
problems.evidence_notes: The Indian journal record supports the pest as a possibility; do not extrapolate outbreak prevalence.

problems.display_title: Drooping/pale leaves or shoot dieback

possible_causes.cause: Watering/root stress is a possibility, especially when decline follows frequent watering or repotting
supporting_clues: Soil is wet for long periods
Symptoms began after transplanting or frequent daily watering

possible_causes.cause: Dry-root or heat stress also needs checking
supporting_clues: Soil is dry and pot is exposed to hot sun/wind

follow_up_questions: Is the mix wet or dry below the surface?
Was the plant recently transplanted or pruned heavily?
Does the pot drain freely?
safe_next_steps: Check moisture and drainage before changing watering frequency.
Avoid keeping roots in standing water; observe new growth after changing one factor at a time.
Ask a knowledgeable local nursery/extension service if stem dieback progresses.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not use a fixed daily watering schedule.
Do not state root rot is confirmed from drooping alone.
problems.evidence_notes: The curry-leaf case source is anecdotal and its responder explicitly framed overwatering as a possibility; further India-specific diagnostic sourcing is needed.

problems.display_title: Yellow leaves or yellow/soft stem

possible_causes.cause: Excess moisture/water quality/root stress
supporting_clues: Soil is waterlogged or roots remain stagnant
Stem is soft or rotting
Water-grown setup is not refreshed regularly

follow_up_questions: Is it grown in soil or water?
If in water, when was it last changed?
Is the yellow section firm or soft?
safe_next_steps: For water culture, refresh water regularly and inspect roots/container.
For soil culture, check moisture and make sure excess water drains.
Remove a badly rotting cutting only if healthy material remains and follow propagation guidance.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not treat soil-grown and water-grown plants as having identical care needs.
Do not assume every yellow leaf proves disease.

problems.display_title: Brown tips or visible pests

possible_causes.cause: Low humidity or moisture/environmental stress
supporting_clues: Tip browning without visible insects

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs, mites or scale
supporting_clues: Cottony material, webbing or fixed raised bumps

follow_up_questions: Are pests or webbing visible?
Is the plant grown indoors near dry airflow?
Is water culture refreshed regularly?
safe_next_steps: Inspect leaves/stems and clean the container if grown in water.
Check its growing setup and avoid sudden harsh sun.
Identify any pest before treatment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not infer low humidity if pest evidence is present.

problems.display_title: Yellowing or dropping leaves

possible_causes.cause: Overwatering, cold draft/temperature drop or environmental stress
supporting_clues: Several leaves drop after a cold draft or move
Soil remains wet
Symptoms follow a sudden temperature change

possible_causes.cause: Normal ageing of some lower leaves
supporting_clues: Only occasional bottom leaves yellow and drop while upper growth remains healthy

follow_up_questions: Are mainly the oldest bottom leaves affected?
Was there a recent move, draft or temperature change?
Is the mix wet or dry?
safe_next_steps: Review light, temperature and moisture together.
Keep its location stable and protect it from cold drafts.
Check whether the pattern spreads to new growth.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not interpret one old lower leaf dropping as a confirmed disease.
Do not automatically increase watering after leaf drop.

problems.display_title: Sticky leaves, cottony clusters or webbing

possible_causes.cause: Mealybugs, scale or spider mites
supporting_clues: Cottony wax on leaf joints/undersides
Fixed bumps on stems/leaves
Fine webbing and stippling

follow_up_questions: Can you see cottony material, bumps or webbing?
Are leaf undersides affected?
Are nearby plants showing similar signs?
safe_next_steps: Isolate and inspect the plant carefully.
Wipe dust from leaves and confirm pest identity before choosing treatment.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not apply unverified DIY sprays that can damage leaves.

problems.display_title: Brown patches or sudden leaf damage

possible_causes.cause: Harsh direct afternoon sun, cold drafts or abrupt environment change
supporting_clues: Damage appears after moving into stronger sun or exposure to cold air

follow_up_questions: Was the plant moved or exposed to direct afternoon sun?
Was it near an air conditioner, open window or cold draft?
safe_next_steps: Use bright indirect light/partial shade and keep temperatures stable.
Acclimate gradually when changing light exposure.
avoid_recommending_without_more_evidence: Do not assume brown patches are a contagious disease without other clues.
